chapter: The House That Jazz Built and Homestead childhood
title: Political consciousness and Black participation in Homestead politics
summary: She became politically active later; Homestead had a Burgess, and few Black people held jobs beyond mill work.

empassioned -- I won't say political activist, a community activist anyway, you must have learned this kind of political consciousness somewhere.

Not really, I really didn't get into that until -- that's been since I've been here in New York in the Bronx. And this all started, I suppose, at the time when I got involved with the Parents Association and then the local council, the East Bronx Community Council, and I would say this must have started in 1957.
Do you have any recollection about the political organization of Homestead? Specifically the participation of Blacks.
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943

Yeah, well, in Homestead we had a Burgess -- Homestead was a very small borough, I believe when I was going to school the population of Homestead must have been about 18,000 and it was an independent borough, it wasn't connected to Pittsburgh at the time. But there was always quite a bit of activity at election time. There's a possibility that my grandmother on my father's side, might have been politically active, but I wouldn't know about that. So far as I can remember -- you see, the neighborhoods were not segregated. At one time we lived in I guess what you would call a multiple dwelling, three or four families, with a Hungarian family, with a Polish family and we didn't exactly feel, you know, that there was segregation there. There might have been segregation between the so-called affluent and so-called poor. We were among the poor class of people because we were workers. There were not that many other occupations in Homestead unless it might have been -- you might have had a store or something like that.

There were probably some clerks. It didn't appear to me there was that much local government where one could be employed as a civil servant, except for the police department, sanitation, and things like that. You know, two railroads ran through Homestead. The Pennsylvania Railroad and the Pittsburgh and Lake Erie. The coal mines were real adjacent to Homestead, I'd say within a radius of 30 miles you would be in the coal mining region. That's just about what that was like. The so-called affluent, Black or white, would probably have been foremen or whatever the higher ups in the hierarchy, working in the mill. You know they had to have overseers and things like that. And I suppose, too, the families that got there first would be the ones who would have had what you call tenure or been in the mill longer. So they would move up the ladder. That's just about it. After I left high school --
